content: 1. Grants or financial awards often provide school leaders with autonomy in how they allocate funds. While this flexibility is beneficial for implementing health-promoting school (HPS) activities, it is generally insufficient for long-term resource allocation and does not support the sustainability of HPS initiatives. 2. Financial support from national or local governments, as well as non-governmental organizations, is crucial during the early stages of local policy development and the institutional embedding of HPS programs. 3. The capacity of a school to implement HPS requires both relational and organizational support. This includes allocating time for curriculum planning and implementation. However, barriers such as insufficient resources for staff leadership and management, lack of staff capacity, limited staff time, and inadequate resources to seek external support hinder effective implementation. 4. Access to expertise from external health promotion professionals can provide critical support to school staff, facilitate the implementation of HPS, and aid in the evaluation of these initiatives. Sustained support from health professionals, such as school nurses and counselors, is essential for the successful implementation and maintenance of many HPS programs. 5. Evidence-informed practices should guide all activities related to planning and designing HPS initiatives in schools. This involves collecting and synthesizing research and evidence to inform evidence-based approaches, such as communities of practice, for school implementation. 6. Certification programs can formally recognize schools as health-promoting schools, providing a structured framework for evaluating and accrediting their efforts. 7. In Paraguay, the Healthy School Strategy (HSS) is a participatory process that considers the unique needs and potential of each school. It is led by local, regional, and national health and education departments, with involvement from other sectors and stakeholders. 8. The HSS process begins with a situational analysis conducted by school authorities and the school community, including students. A management team is then formed, comprising representatives from the educational community, health sector, and other community members, such as municipal officials and private sector representatives. 9. A participatory appraisal is conducted, followed by the development of an action plan tailored to each school. Progress is monitored using indicators defined within the HSS framework. 10. Schools can achieve accreditation as a quality healthy school by meeting criteria and indicators verified by the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare. Certification provides formal recognition of the school as a healthy school by the WHO Regional Office for the Americas. 11. In Ireland, well-being is integrated into the secondary school curriculum as a subject and is also embedded across all other school subjects. Primary schools can develop their own well-being programs using various curriculum components. 12. Ireland’s Wellbeing Policy Statement and Framework for Practice (2018–2023) emphasizes the integration of well-being into every school policy and curriculum. It sets goals for promoting well-being in schools and provides indicators of success in areas such as culture, curriculum, policy, and relationships. 13. Teacher training and professional learning are essential for equipping educators to deliver curricula that promote health and well-being. This includes pre-service and in-service training tailored to the specific needs of teachers in different countries. 14. Professional learning should cover topics such as life skills, mental health, sexuality education, healthy diet promotion, and physical activity. It should also include strategies for managing public health emergencies, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. 15. The professionalization of teachers and school leaders for HPS implementation depends on the teaching workforce and career pathway structures in each country.
